scope_reason: Direct preregistered controlled evaluation of feedback-driven Harness search, including GEPA-selected prompts and audit/attribution of reported gains. The evaluation design itself need not be an evolving agent.
source_protocol: Only prompt text is searched in the GEPA arms; selections use train/validation and locked replication/test partitions. The paper explicitly studies one round of selection and no recursive loop.

version_comparison.boundary: 65 and 7/12 remain valid only with the first-two-studies qualifier in v3. They do not describe v1 or the entire three-study v3 paper. Do not invent a whole-paper total by merging heterogeneous statuses.

current_canonical_snapshot.summary_en: Preregistered study: harness search gains from unreadable answers, weak comparisons, evaluation flaws; 65 primary endpoints; thinking-off raised accuracy in 7 of 12 model-benchmark units, mainly capped thinking lacking readable answers.

summary_findings.finding: Canonical version remains 1 but the stored summary cites 65 primary endpoints and 7 of 12 cells; official v1 gives 47 and 5 of 9. A paper version and its summarized evidence must be selected and bound together.

If formally moving to v3, describe three studies and qualify 65/7-of-12 as the first two; the third adds its own registered endpoints and statuses. Positive FPB results rule out a blanket claim that all Harness gains only repair visibility.
Keep harness_eval rather than claiming a demonstrated recursive self-improvement method; the source explicitly says one round of selection and no recursive loop.

quotes.quote: Abstract Harness search keeps a change to the prompts, reasoning switches, token budgets or parsers around a frozen model if the change raises a score. Such a gain can come from answers the parser could not read before, a weak comparison, or a defect in the evaluation. We preregistered a study of where these gains come from, with three small models, three benchmarks, replication and test partitions, a GEPA search arm and six evaluation defects injected one at a time, and we report all 47 primary endpoints. Turning thinking off raised accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 5 of 9 model-benchmark cells, and in each the gain came mostly from questions where the capped setting gave no readable answer. The thinking-off setting was not meaningfully worse than a rescue configuration or four GEPA-selected harnesses in 11 of 13 comparisons, and lost to the rescue on GSM8K for two models. GEPA repaired its broken starting points, but none of its selected harnesses was more accurate than the thinking-off setting. A thinking budget in the serving engine, which also allows a longer answer, lowered truncation and raised the parse rate in 6 of 9 cells. In 6 of 15 evaluable defect-model pairs, replication through the same pipeline reproduced the defect’s distortion instead of revealing it. On the LongevityBench multiple-choice tasks, only the longevity-tuned model beat the strongest constant-label baseline.

Abstract A harness search around a frozen longevity-tuned 1.7B model reported a rescue. An audit found that the gain came from rows the start left unparsed, that the caller sent each row’s reference answer as an assistant turn, and that replication through the same pipeline missed it. Is a harness’s gain more than a constant answer would give? We preregistered three studies and report every endpoint. In the first two, thinking off raised test accuracy over a capped thinking setting in 7 of 12 cells, mostly on rows the cap left unparsed. It was not meaningfully worse than a rescue in 7 of 9 small-model test cells or than four GEPA harnesses at 1.7B. Replication reproduced an injected defect’s distortion in 9 of 20 evaluable cases (7 fixed by design). At 14B, two GEPA harnesses beat thinking off by 34 points on test but were not detectably above the strongest constant label, and answered “Yes” in 94.6% and 98.2% of parsed mortality answers on test. In the third study (SmolLM3-3B, base Qwen3-1.7B), GEPA beat the constant on FPB (confirmatory, both partitions); thinking off was not meaningfully worse than any BoolQ harness, and 3 of 4 MMLU-Pro searches kept their seed (the fourth inconclusive on test). On Autocast (exploratory), the harnesses were within 0.7 points of the constant and gave one label in 93.1% to 96.8% of parsed answers, both on test. On questions about the input or about knowledge (FPB, BoolQ, MMLU-Pro), GEPA beat the constant or found no clear gain over thinking off; on questions that ask for a prediction (14B mortality, descriptive; Autocast, exploratory), the harness ended near the constant and gave one label almost throughout while its gain over thinking off looked large. The constant label told the two apart wherever the gain was large. This rests on few tasks that also differ in label skew, number of labels and task type, so it is not shown to depend on the kind of question.

We ask what a harness repairs in three preregistered studies, each frozen before any call on its replication and test partitions. The first, frozen on 30 September 2026 at 06:53:11 UTC, uses three models of 1.7B to 8B parameters, three benchmark pools, an adaptive arm in which GEPA ( Agrawal et al., 2025 ) searches for harnesses around the 1.7B model, and six evaluation defects injected one at a time. The second, frozen on 7 October 2026 at 00:28:49 UTC after the first study’s results were known, puts the same hypotheses to Qwen3-14B with a GEPA arm of its own, and reruns the base and the tuned version of Qwen3-1.7B on a second GPU as a descriptive comparison. The third, frozen on 26 October 2026 at 09:16:03 UTC, tests whether what we found around the longevity model holds on other benchmarks and models: SmolLM3-3B and base Qwen3-1.7B on BoolQ, FPB and MMLU-Pro, a new hypothesis that compares each harness with the constant label, and Autocast as an exploratory arm (Figure 1 b and c).

The results cover five models, one of which is the tuned model that the case study searched around, six benchmarks and six defects, and nothing beyond them; the pattern across the studies rests on few tasks (Section 7.6 ). We studied one round of selection and no recursive loop. We do not claim that harness gains can be illusory, that thinking off can beat a thinking cap, or that agent and harness evaluations can be preregistered, since each has been shown or done before, and we do not claim that harness search finds genuine quality gains in general.

Table 2 states the four hypotheses. The first study has 47 primary endpoints and the second 18, 65 in all; they are the only confirmatory results, and their verdicts come from percentile-bootstrap intervals adjusted within each family.

In the second study visibility dominates again where the capped setting leaves rows unparsed. Visibility dominates on the letters ( Δ = + 0.203 \Delta=+0.203 [ + 0.186 +0.186 , + 0.219 +0.219 ]) and on MMLU-Pro ( Δ = + 0.402 \Delta=+0.402 [ + 0.350 +0.350 , + 0.453 +0.453 ]), and the gate fails on GSM8K ( Δ = − 0.241 \Delta=-0.241 [ − 0.315 -0.315 , − 0.167 -0.167 ]). In the letter cell the parse pattern fixes the quantity: THINK-512 parses 0.001 of the letter rows and every unparsed call ended at the token limit, so B holds 2 of 3,942 rows, Δ B \Delta_{B} is 0.000 0.000 and the whole gain is visibility; the verdict still rests on the gate and on the interval of T T . On GSM8K AUTHORS-1500 is less accurate than THINK-512 on the rows both configurations parse, the pattern of Intern-S1-mini : T = + 0.293 T=+0.293 is positive only because Δ B \Delta_{B} is large and negative, the reading the gate exists to stop (Appendix M ). Over both studies visibility dominates in 7 of 12 cells.

GEPA runs as in the earlier studies, with Intern-S1-mini as the proposer, on a clean start only and on prompt text only: a system prompt and an appended instruction. Each model and benchmark has one seed harness, an empty system prompt and no instruction, so four per model; its requests equal those of AUTHORS-1500 on every row of its sample (text and token ids, checked before each run). Each pair has two search seeds, so there are 16 runs: twelve on BoolQ, FPB and MMLU-Pro, and four on Autocast. A run spends 6,000 metric calls on a 300-row sample of the search partition, half for training and half for validation, and the harness with the highest mean validation score is selected (ties to the lowest candidate index, and the seed if no proposal was accepted). Each selected harness is then evaluated on the replication partition and, after a checkpoint that locks it and is committed before the first test call, on the test partition. A check that a thinking-off call does not begin with the model’s own thinking token (gate (b)) stops the grid and, as decided after the freeze, records in the searches and in the evaluations of selected harnesses (Section 8 ).

The families are fixed at 4, 12 and 8 endpoints (levels 98.75%, 99.58% and 99.375%) whatever the screening shows. H1 has one endpoint per model and kept benchmark, H2 one per model, benchmark (the two kept ones and MMLU-Pro) and seed, and H5 one per model, kept benchmark and seed. The analysis report’s own summary field gives the H5 family as 4, the number of confirmatory H5 endpoints; the preregistration fixes it at 8, and the report gives the confirmatory H5 endpoints the adjusted interval of that family of 8, which is what we use; its descriptive and exploratory H5 estimates carry unadjusted 95% intervals. Of the 40 endpoints of the study, 20 are confirmatory, 10 descriptive and 10 exploratory. MMLU-Pro is descriptive for H1 and H5, because the gain of AUTHORS-1500 over THINK-512 is known from the first two studies; its H2 is confirmatory, because the harnesses are new and its search items were never called. Descriptive endpoints carry the unadjusted interval, and a statement that combines endpoints is confirmatory only if each of them is. Fixed in advance and reported next to every H5 verdict, without changing any verdict, are the label collapse (at least 90% of the harness’s parsed test answers are the majority label) and four flags: a literal constant predictor, no accepted proposal in the run, identical selected harnesses for the two seeds, and pervasive parse failure.

All 4 confirmatory endpoints, which are the FPB harnesses, are above the constant on both partitions and replicated: Δ c \Delta_{c} lies between 14.2 and 19.8 points over both partitions, against the constant “neutral”. The descriptive endpoints agree: BoolQ’s harnesses are 14.5 to 22.5 points above the constant “yes” and MMLU-Pro’s 22.1 to 28.5 points above the search partition’s constant (“A”; the oracle constant on test is B), over both partitions. Three of the four MMLU-Pro harnesses are the seed, so for them H5 says that AUTHORS-1500 itself is above the constant. All 12 H5 endpoints that carry a verdict are above the constant on both partitions (24 verdicts), and none is at the constant , below or inconclusive . The 14B pattern, H2 fails with H5 at the constant , therefore occurs in no confirmatory or descriptive cell. The four FPB harnesses show the opposite: H2 fails and H5 is above the constant , both confirmatory, so a search found a harness that beats the baseline and the constant label. No harness of BoolQ, FPB or MMLU-Pro collapses onto the majority label: 0 of 24 cells (twelve harnesses on two partitions) reach the collapse threshold, with majority shares of 11.8% to 68.6% of parsed answers on test and 12.3% to 70.5% on replication.

This paper contributes methodology for evaluating harness search and the pipelines that report it: a preregistered design, audit checks and a record of what each result rests on. It builds no new capability, since the models and benchmarks are public and the benchmark behind the longevity tasks derives from public survey data, and the accuracies, those of small and mid-sized models on research tasks, do not support any use of these models for medical advice or clinical decisions. One misreading to avoid is that a thinking-off baseline is always enough, and the studies show cells in which it is not.
